profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab that is reproducing and extending Neural SPH for long-horizon particle-fluid rollouts. Over the past three days, the team’s current 'V2' setup has started showing particle clustering and rapidly growing rollout error on the 2D dam-break and rotating-column benchmarks, despite looking normal in routine validation. They have one remaining window on a shared A100 node this afternoon and want to decide which single targeted test to run before the allocation expires. The agenda is to compare the current failing setup against what each person considers the previously good 'V2' reference, identify the most plausible source of the regression, and agree on one minimally disruptive fix to try today. The expected outcome is a concrete troubleshooting plan consisting of one config/code change and one confirmatory run, not a broader redesign of the model or benchmark suite.

members.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
members.expertise: Physics-informed graph neural networks, learned particle simulators, long-horizon rollout analysis
members.background: Lena leads the lab’s neural simulation work and built the group’s internal Neural SPH-style extensions, especially the pressure and viscosity corrections used to suppress tensile-instability clustering during long rollouts.
members.private_state: She wants to recover the long-horizon result quickly using the current checkpoint family so they can update figures for an upcoming submission, and she wants to avoid opening a larger infrastructure investigation that could consume the rest of the week.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says a model is 'stable,' the obvious meaning is that an open-loop rollout stays visually and quantitatively well-behaved for the full 1000-step benchmark window without clustering.

The 'V2 baseline' is the lab’s colloquial name for the post-optimization internal setup she has been using in recent plots, notes, and slide decks, so everyone must be referring to that same artifact.

If they decide to 'put the SPH correction back in,' the natural minimal interpretation is to re-enable the correction only in rollout-time dynamics on top of the existing checkpoint rather than altering training behavior.
A quick correction pass that touches the checkpoint should mean a short warm-start calibration run of the force head plus the rollout test, not a fresh multi-day retraining job.

The old pressure coefficient was already meaningful in normalized simulation units tied to particle spacing, so reusing the same numeric value should still be valid unless the physical regime itself changed.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Simulation data pipelines, experiment infrastructure, graph construction, reproducible ML systems
members.background: Arjun maintains the lab’s training and evaluation stack and recently unified the fluid benchmarks under a common 'V2' config path, including rollout logging, neighbor-list handling, and lightweight checkpoint adaptation utilities.
members.private_state: He wants to pin the regression on something systematic in the pipeline rather than on hand-tuned physics heuristics, because he is trying to leave behind a cleaner and more reproducible codebase for incoming lab members.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the model needs to be 'stable again,' they usually mean the validation dashboard returns to its normal range on the standard 400-step evaluation with periodic state refresh, since that is the lab’s day-to-day health check.
The 'V2 baseline' refers to the archived W&B run tagged v2_stable that became the reference artifact during the refactor, so mentioning 'V2' should unambiguously point to that run.

If they agree to 'put the SPH correction back in,' the correction should be restored in the same pathway the current checkpoint consumes, which in practice means using the warm-start adaptation routine so the force residual is re-aligned before rollout.
A 'quick patch' can reasonably include a 20-30 minute warm-start adaptation pass, because in this codebase that is operationally part of making a checkpoint compatible with a dynamics change.

The pressure coefficient belongs to the raw simulator-unit convention coming from the dataset generator, and feature normalization happens downstream, so the same numeric coefficient should still be appropriate unless the raw data export changed.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a stable rollout
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about getting the model 'stable again.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means no visible tensile-instability clustering and no catastrophic drift over the full 1000-step open-loop benchmark rollout used for paper figures.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means validation metrics returning to the expected range on the lab’s standard 400-step evaluation protocol with periodic state refreshes from ground truth.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In healthy experiments those two notions usually move together, so 'stable' functions as routine shorthand and neither person expects it to hide a different horizon and reset policy.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'V2 baseline' they are comparing against
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to matching 'the V2 baseline.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the post-neighbor-cache internal setup she has been calling 'V2' in slides and local experiment folders, which produced the long clean rollouts she cares about.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the W&B artifact tagged v2_stable from the unified pipeline refactor, which he informally calls 'the V2 baseline' in infra discussions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are genuinely and routinely called 'V2' inside the lab, so the phrase sounds uniquely identifying even though each person silently points to a different reference object.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'put the SPH correction back in' includes
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'put the SPH correction back in' as today’s fix.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means re-enable the SPH correction only during rollout on the current checkpoint, optionally with a tiny compatibility tweak, so they can test whether the added physics term alone suppresses clustering.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means restore the correction through the checkpoint’s active dynamics path by running the standard warm-start adaptation routine before rollout, because in his view that is part of putting the correction back into the current setup.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations fit the lab’s notion of a same-afternoon 'quick fix' and use the same high-level config language, so the difference in pipeline stage stays hidden under shared operational shorthand.

misalignment_points.topic: How to interpret the reused pressure coefficient
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say they can use 'the same pressure coefficient as before.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the coefficient was previously tuned in normalized simulation units scaled by particle spacing, so copying the numeric value into the current branch is valid for the same spacing regime.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the coefficient is defined in raw simulator units from the dataset generator and that normalization does not affect the force code path, so copying the same numeric value is valid for that reason.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The coefficient value is familiar, has already circulated across configs, and both believe the unit convention was settled long ago, so neither sees any reason to reopen the interpretation of that number.
